body:
Every streamed update re-parsed the whole reply and re-rendered every element in it (links with their tooltips, list items, code), so a long reply got more expensive with each delta.

While a reply streams, `ChatMarkdown` now splits it at blank lines that close every open block and renders each block through its own memoized react-markdown. Finished blocks keep their render; only the last one re-parses. Text with syntax that ties blocks together (reference definitions, footnotes, raw HTML, `:::` directives, `$$` math) still renders whole, and so does the finished reply, whose first block React reuses. A test renders every prefix of each sample both ways and compares the HTML.

The renderer context also rebuilt its file-link maps from the full text on every update, which re-rendered every block's links. They are now keyed by the file links found, so streamed text that adds none keeps them stable.

The stream render scenario now asserts one paragraph render per delta (465 on main, 30 here).

### Benchmark

Measured with the [PandaCode vs T3 Code streaming bench](https://github.com/aicodeking/pandacode/tree/main/bench/t3-compare) (W1: a 50 KB Markdown reply delivered as 500 whole-text updates over 32 s, production build, headless Chromium on cups, median of 3 runs). Each row adds one layer of this stack:

| T3 build | Main-thread task | Script | Worst delivery lateness |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| main | 21.0 s | 14.8 s | 73 ms |
| + timeline rows (this stack, 1) | 19.3 s | 13.0 s | 26 ms |
| + Markdown blocks (2) | 12.1 s | 4.4 s | 10 ms |
| + git actions panel (3) | 10.4 s | 3.4 s | 9 ms |
| + streamed text bypasses the timeline (4) | 9.5 s | 2.6 s | 9 ms |
| PandaCode, same machine | 6.6 s | 0.5 s | 2 ms |

The bench delivers an update every 64 ms. In the app the default `paragraph` streaming mode sends at most one every 400 ms, so real streams hit these paths less often, but each update costs what it does here.

Implemented by Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, running in T3 Code.
